newsitem.title: PERU: Sick police chief freed in Peruvian hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Sick police chief freed in Peruvian hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding VIP hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence freed a sick police chief early on Sunday, but his release did little to reduce tensions in the 40-day standoff.

The Red Cross identified the freed hostage as National Police General Jose Rivas Rodriguez, who was wheeled out of the compound on a stretcher flanked by Red Cross officials and Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
Lying face up with his bare feet sticking out from under a blanket, Rodriguez was taken to an ambulance and driven to a nearby police hospital.
International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Mining said the rebels agreed to free Rodriguez on medical grounds. He did not say what was wrong wth him.
The heavily-armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels are still holding 72 hostages.

Rodriguez was the first hostage to be freed since Jan. 17 and his release followed a day of tense posturing with rebels firing warning shots into the air in response to what they called provocative movements by the police outside.

Armoured vehicles have moved in on the residence twice, a police helicopter has flown over the compound and troops have periodically taken up positions around the perimeter wall with guns trained on the building.
Even after the latest rebel shots, the helicopter again made several passes over the residence on Saturday.
The Red Cross said the two shots fired in the afternoon caused no injuries. "We ask for calm so as not to put any lives at risk," Red Cross representative Ruben Ortega said.

In an apparent effort to calm nerves, the government vowed to seek a peaceful end to the crisis. "We are going to take the time needed to reach a peaceful solution to this crisis without bloodshed," Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said.
But he gave no clue as to how the government hoped to end the standoff, which has stalled over its refusal to consider the MRTA's main demand for the release of 400 jailed comrades.
President Alberto Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro remains among the captives, also sought to defuse tension, insisting the police were just doing their job of patrolling.
"What we need is a period with not much talking but time for everyone to reflect," he told a news conference after a two-hour meeting with government negotiator, Domingo Palermo.

While firmly rejecting rebel demands to set their comrades free, Fujimori has offered the roughly 15 hostage-takers safe passage to another country if they lay down their weapons and release all the hostages.
Palermo said he had held a preliminary meeting with a commission of "guarantors" who will oversee eventual talks.
"The Red Cross is preparing for the MRTA to eventually come out for the start of conversations," he said. "I am going to be very clear. There is no deadlock."
The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages Dec. 17 during a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion but have freed most of them in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, congressmen, judges, police and army chiefs, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Red Cross officials have repeatedly said the remaining hostages' health was stable despite claims from individual family members and colleagues that some were sick.
